records.title: Decision on the prevention of and fight against psychological and sexual harassment
records.summary: The Commission’s current anti-harassment policy for its own staff. It replaces the 2006 decision, creates a Chief Confidential Counsellor as the first contact point for people who feel harassed, and sets out the informal and formal procedures.

records.title: A comprehensive approach to mental health
records.summary: Sets out the Commission’s mental health policy across sectors, including psychosocial risks and mental health at work. It is a policy programme, not binding law.

records.title: EU strategic framework on health and safety at work 2021–2027
records.summary: The Commission’s priorities for occupational safety and health for all workers in the EU, including the prevention of psychosocial risks. It is a policy programme, not binding law.

records.title: Decision on how the EEAS dealt with allegations of psychological harassment in an EU civilian mission
records.summary: An example of the Ombudsman reviewing how an institution handled a staff member’s harassment allegations, here in the EUCAP Sahel Mali mission. The case was settled by the institution; the full decision is not published, to protect the complainant.

records.title: Report on dignity at work in the EU institutions and agencies
records.summary: Reviews the anti-harassment policies of 26 EU institutions and agencies and lists good practices: awareness raising, mandatory training, psychosocial risk assessment, swift procedures, and cover for all personnel including trainees.

records.title: Staff Regulations of Officials and Conditions of Employment of Other Servants
records.summary: Article 12a prohibits psychological and sexual harassment and protects staff who report it. Article 24 obliges the institution to assist staff who are attacked or harassed. Articles 22a and 22b protect whistleblowers, and Article 1e requires working conditions that meet health and safety standards.

decisions.title: Decision on the European Commission’s refusal to give public access to documents concerning the follow-up to an OLAF investigation (case 132/2025/ACB)

decisions.summary: The OLAF evaluation discusses inconsistent interpretations of OLAF powers in matters involving EU staff, including harassment, and identifies questions around whistleblower and informant safeguards. It is an oversight report, not a determination of an individual harassment complaint.

explainerParagraphs: Budgetary discharge is Parliament’s annual political scrutiny of how EU money was managed and implemented. Parliament reviews the accounts, audit findings, recommendations and the responsible institutions’ answers before deciding whether to grant, postpone or refuse discharge.

Article 319(3) TFEU requires the Commission to take appropriate steps on observations in discharge decisions and to report on those measures when requested. The Financial Regulation sets the follow-up framework and its timetable. Read the Treaty provision (opens the official source in a new tab) and Financial Regulation 2024/2509 (opens the official source in a new tab).
It is a budget accountability process. It is separate from staff or employment procedures, and a discharge decision does not by itself establish that every irregularity has been resolved.
